Myths that sound scientific

"Sugar makes children hyperactive"

Many parents believe it, but blind studies do not show it. What changes is how adults see them.

At birthdays and parties, children's excitement is often blamed on sweets. The idea became popular in the 1970s.

Blind studies

In 1995, a meta-analysis by Mark Wolraich pooled 16 studies in which children were given sugar or a sweetener without them or their parents knowing which. No differences in behaviour or attention were found, including in children with ADHD.

Another study showed the role of expectations: some mothers were told their sons had had lots of sugar, although they had actually been given a placebo. Those mothers rated their sons as more hyperactive, watched them more closely and criticised them more. What probably winds children up at a party is the party. There are other good reasons to limit sugar, such as dental health and weight.

References

  1. Wolraich, M. L., Wilson, D. B. y White, J. W. (1995). The effect of sugar on behavior or cognition in children. JAMA, 274(20), 1617–1621.
  2. Hoover, D. W. y Milich, R. (1994). Effects of sugar ingestion expectancies on mother-child interactions. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology, 22(4), 501–515.
